newsitem.title: FINLAND: NATO's Solana to break new ground in Finland.
newsitem.headline: NATO's Solana to break new ground in Finland.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana will dismantle one of the last Cold War barriers on Wednesday when he makes the first official visit by a head of the Western alliance to formerly isolated Finland.

The trip, which also includes a first visit to neutral Sweden, is not likely to herald any sudden bids by the European Union newcomers to join the queue for the expanded alliance. But Finnish officials expect a frank discussion of that project.

For Finland, which fidgeted for decades in a "mutual friendship pact" with the former Soviet Union and only recently started to re-examine its militarily neutral stance, enlargement of NATO raises nuts-and-bolts questions.

"It's not that we are concerned about Russian opposition -- enlargement as such is none of our business," said one senior official. "What we emphasise always is the importance of a parallel development in NATO-Russian relations."

A plan by NATO -- the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation -- to seal a charter with Russia as part of its eastward enlargement, due to be settled by 1999, has reassured the Finns. But they will nonetheless underline its importance.
"Russia has to be included in the process -- because without Russia, there's no lasting security process to be built in Europe," said the official, who asked not be named.

At the popular level, many in this country of 5.1 million still fear the Russian "bear" they twice fought back over their 800-mile (1,300 km) border in World War Two. But if Finland's leaders still see Russia as a bear, it is a wounded one.
Trade with neighbouring Russia is only slowly reviving after the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1990 left Finland seeking new buyers for about one-fifth of its exports.
Its eastern neighbour is still heavily in Finland's debt after its share of Finnish exports slumped from over 20 percent in 1984 to about five percent 10 years later.

Finland, perched between Russia to its east and the edgy former Soviet Baltic States to the south, is pleased with NATO's proposal to beef up its Partnership for Peace scheme for countries left out of enlargement's first wave.

"We have been expressing concern about Baltic security -- this is one of the ways of taking care of that," the official said, alluding to a wide view among diplomats that Estonia, Lithuania and Latvia will not be among the first in NATO.

But at the same time, the Finnish politicians Solana meets, from President Martti Ahtisaari to Defence Minister Anneli Taina, are likely to stress that they would prefer Partnership for Peace to be developed and run centrally, not regionally.

"We think it's important that each region is anchored very strongly in the centre," the official said. "Obviously there will be regional practical exercises, but we don't want the Baltic-Nordic area to become disconnected from the whole."
Helsinki has warned that if Russia turned nationalist, it might attempt to re-annexe the Baltic states which still have large Russian minorities.
Finns are concerned at some suggestions that Finland and Sweden offer security guarantees for the Baltics -- a notion seen as impractical and absurd by Russia's relatively tiny neighbour.
"To put it bluntly," the source said, "we do not want to left with the baby in our arms."
